question: On 14 March 2023, Parliament adopted its position on the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (2021/0426 (COD)), which was then submitted for interinstitutional negotiations pursuant to Rule 59(4).

In the last of the negotiations, on 7 December 2023, a compromise text was produced, the legislative procedure for which will conclude on Parliament’s side with the vote in the committee responsible and then in plenary.

The new text, assuming it goes through, has a section on penalties in Article 31, which reads: ‘Member States shall lay down the rules on penalties applicable to infringements of the national provisions adopted pursuant to this Directive and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that they are implemented. The penalties provided for shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.’ In view of the above: 1.

Even if they fall within the competence of the Member States, are these ‘effective, proportionate and dissuasive’ penalties not likely to hit the most vulnerable and energy-poor citizens hardest, for whom there are no specific safeguards or exemptions?

Could the application of a penalty system under the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive not have a negative social impact and ultimately hinder the attainment of the final energy efficiency targets?
answer: The provisional agreement on the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive recast does not provide an obligation on individual homeowners to renovate their homes and neither does it target individual residential buildings. Each Member State will establish its own trajectory to improve the energy performance of the national residential buildings stock, allowing to address their national characteristics.

Thus, Member States have the flexibility to set up appropriate measures to ensure that the residential building stock will reduce the average energy consumption by 16% in 2030 and between 20-22% in 2035, while providing financial and technical assistance to vulnerable households.

Finally, Member States need to consider the needs of vulnerable households when establishing penalties, which must not only be effective and dissuasive, but also proportionate. Article 31 of the provisional agreement provides a text on penalties, widely used in EU Directives to ensure compliance with the EU acquis.
